content: Blood tests are laboratory procedures performed on blood samples to assess disease states and evaluate the function of various organs. Blood circulates throughout the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients while removing waste products to be excreted. Consequently, the condition of the bloodstream is both influenced by and reflective of numerous medical conditions. For this reason, blood tests are among the most frequently conducted medical diagnostic tools. Blood is typically collected from a vein via venipuncture or from a fingertip using a finger prick, except in cases such as arterial blood gas tests, which require arterial blood. Blood sampling is considered a relatively non-invasive method to obtain cells and extracellular fluid (plasma) for health evaluation. Although the term blood test is commonly used, most routine tests (excluding many hematology tests) are performed on plasma or serum rather than whole blood. A basic metabolic panel measures levels of sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), magnesium, creatinine, and glucose. Calcium is sometimes included in this panel. While a standard glucose test measures blood sugar at a single point in time, a glucose tolerance test involves repeated measurements to evaluate how efficiently the body processes glucose. Most of these tests are conducted using venous blood. In contrast, arterial blood gas tests are performed on arterial blood, which makes the procedure more invasive, uncomfortable, and potentially risky. Protein analysis in blood can involve techniques such as protein electrophoresis and Western blotting, which are general methods rather than specific tests. Liver function tests are also used to assess protein-related parameters. Antibody proteins can be evaluated through serology techniques, including the Wassermann test (for syphilis), ELISA, and the Coombs test. DNA testing, made possible even with minimal blood quantities, is widely used in forensic science and increasingly in diagnosing various disorders. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a common method for DNA analysis, while Northern blotting is used for RNA detection. Cellular components of blood are analyzed through tests such as the full blood count (or complete blood count), hematocrit, and mean corpuscular volume (MCV). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is another test used to assess inflammation. Cross-matching is performed to determine blood type compatibility for transfusions or organ transplants. Blood cultures are often obtained when an infection is suspected. Positive cultures, along with sensitivity results, are critical in guiding appropriate medical treatment.
